- If sentiment is positive (≥ 0.5) in the recent history, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ -0.5) or flat, model often underestimates; adjust downward bias or increase volatility buffer.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots; apply a “cool-down” correction to prevent overreaction.
- Model consistently overpredicts early in the 30-day horizon when sentiment is neutral or slightly positive — reduce initial forecast values by 1–2%.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below forecast), model may be lagging — adjust for delayed reaction to sentiment shifts.
- When sentiment history shows a recent spike followed by flat or negative sentiment, model often fails to correct — apply a “sentiment decay” rule to dampen forecast growth.
- Forecast should not exceed 3–5% above recent 7-day high unless sentiment is strongly bullish — otherwise, cap upward movement to avoid overconfidence bias.
